q-64273.name: Question 1
q-64273.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y=10\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{-x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-64273.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $10\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ So we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)-(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)-2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(-3\alpha -\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(\alpha -3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=10\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha -\beta =10\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \alpha -3\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-3$ and $\beta =-1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

q-8121.name: Question 2
q-8121.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$
q-8121.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=0
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +5 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+5 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1\pm 2\text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)+2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
(4\alpha +2\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(-2\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}4\alpha +2\beta =6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ -2\alpha +4\beta =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1$ and $\beta =1.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is 6cos⁡x+2sin⁡x. Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is yp=αcos⁡x+βsin⁡x, where α and β are constants that are to be determined.

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives: (4α+2β)cos⁡x+(−2α+4β)sin⁡x=6cos⁡x+2sin⁡x

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations: {4α+2β=6(equating the coefficients ofcos⁡x)−2α+4β=2(equating the coefficients ofsin⁡x)

Solving this system gives α=1 and β=1.

Therefore, the particular integral yp(x) is yp(x)=cos⁡x+sin⁡x.

q-64276.problem:
Find the general solution to the problem

$$
{y}^{″}+y=8\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$
q-64276.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\pm \text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form
y_p = x (\alpha \cos x + \beta \sin x),
]
where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & =2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=8\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x=8\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ -2\alpha =8\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-4$ and $\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-4x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}=P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

q-64276.html:
Question 3
?

Find the general solution to the problem y″+y=8sin⁡x.

a
y=Pcos⁡x+Qsin⁡x−cos⁡x+2sin⁡x
b
y=Pcos⁡x+Qsin⁡x−4xcos⁡x
c
y=Pex+Qe−x+4sin⁡x
d
y=Pex+Qxex−2cos⁡x+6sin⁡x
e
y=Pcos⁡x+Qsin⁡x−2xcos⁡x+6sin⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the complementary function yc(x), which is the solution to the homogeneous equation y″+y=0.

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives: λ2+1=0λ2=−1

So λ=±i, and therefore the complementary function yc(x) is yc=Pcos⁡x+Qsin⁡x.

We now need to find the particular solution yp(x).

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form αcos⁡x+βsin⁡x because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form y_p = x (\alpha \cos x + \beta \sin x), ] where α and β are constants that are to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of yp gives: yp′=(αcos⁡x+βsin⁡x)+x(−αsin⁡x+βcos⁡x)yp″=2(−αsin⁡x+βcos⁡x)+x(−αcos⁡x−βsin⁡x)

To find the values of α and β, we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation: 2(−αsin⁡x+βcos⁡x)+x(−αcos⁡x−βsin⁡x)+x(αcos⁡x+βsin⁡x)=8sin⁡x

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives −2αsin⁡x+2βcos⁡x=8sin⁡x.

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations: {2β=0(equating the coefficients ofcos⁡x)−2α=8(equating the coefficients ofsin⁡x)

Solving this system gives α=−4 and β=0.

Therefore, the particular solution yp(x) is yp(x)=−4xcos⁡x.

The general solution is given by y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x), and therefore, the general solution in our case is y=yc+yp=Pcos⁡x+Qsin⁡x−4xcos⁡x.

q-64274.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4y=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-64274.worked_solution:
The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+2x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =4(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x)-4x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
4(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x)-4x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+4x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\ -4\alpha =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1$ and $\beta =0.$ Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.

q-64274.html:
Question 4
?

Given that the differential equation d2ydx2+4y=−4sin⁡2x has the complementary function yc(x)=Acos⁡2x+Bsin⁡2x, find the particular solution yp(x) to this equation.

a
yp=xcos⁡2x
b
yp=xcos⁡2x+xsin⁡2x
c
yp=xcos⁡2x+2xsin⁡2x
d
yp=xcos⁡2x−xsin⁡2x
e
yp=−2xsin⁡2x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form αcos⁡2x+βsin⁡2x because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form yp=x(αcos⁡2x+βsin⁡2x), where α and β are constants that are to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of yp gives: dypdx=(αcos⁡2x+βsin⁡2x)+2x(−αsin⁡2x+βcos⁡2x)d2ypdx2=4(−αsin⁡2x+βcos⁡2x)−4x(αcos⁡2x+βsin⁡2x)

To find the values of α and β, we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation: 4(−αsin⁡2x+βcos⁡2x)−4x(αcos⁡2x+βsin⁡2x)+4x(αcos⁡2x+βsin⁡2x)=−4sin⁡2x

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives −4αsin⁡2x+4βcos⁡2x=−4sin⁡2x.

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations: {4β=0(equating the coefficients ofcos⁡2x)−4α=−4(equating the coefficients ofsin⁡2x)

Solving this system gives α=1 and β=0. Therefore, the particular solution yp(x) is yp(x)=xcos⁡2x.

q-79633.name: Question 5
q-79633.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-2y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1$ or $\lambda =2$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{2x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {y}^{″} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)-2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
(-3\alpha -\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(\alpha -3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha -\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \alpha -3\beta =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,$ $\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{2x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Now let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B-1=0.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-A{e}^{-x}+2B{e}^{2x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=-1$ into the above gives

$$
-A+2B=-1.
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}A+B=1 \\ -A+2B=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=1,$ $B=0.$
Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{-x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Solve the initial value problem y″−y′−2y=3cos⁡x−sin⁡x,y(0)=0,y′(0)=−1.

a
y=2e2x−sin⁡x−2cos⁡x
b
y=−2e2x+2cos⁡x
c
y=e2x−e−x+sin⁡x
d

e
y=e−x−cos⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the complementary function yc(x), which is the solution to the homogeneous equation y″−y′−2y=0.

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives: λ2−λ−2=0(λ+1)(λ−2)=0

So λ=−1 or λ=2, and therefore the complementary function yc(x) is yc(x)=Ae−x+Be2x.

We now need to find the particular solution yp(x).

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is 3cos⁡x−sin⁡x. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form yp=αcos⁡x+βsin⁡x, where α and β are constants that are to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of yp gives: y′=−αsin⁡x+βcos⁡xy″=−αcos⁡x−βsin⁡x.

To find the values of α and β, we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation: −αcos⁡x−βsin⁡x−(−αsin⁡x+βcos⁡x)−2(αcos⁡x+βsin⁡x)=3cos⁡x−sin⁡x

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives: (−3α−β)cos⁡x+(α−3β)sin⁡x=3cos⁡x−sin⁡x

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations: {−3α−β=3(equating the coefficients ofcos⁡x)α−3β=−1(equating the coefficients ofsin⁡x)

Solving this system gives α=−1, β=0.

Therefore, the particular solution yp(x) is yp(x)=−cos⁡x.

The general solution is given by y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x), and therefore, the general solution in our case is y=Ae−x+Be2x−cos⁡x.

Now let us find constants A and B.

Substituting y(0)=0 into the general solution gives A+B−1=0.

We now need to apply the condition y′(0)=−1. First, we differentiate y to find y′: y′=−Ae−x+2Be2x+sin⁡x

Substituting y′(0)=−1 into the above gives −A+2B=−1.

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for A and B: {A+B=1−A+2B=−1

Solving this system gives A=1, B=0. Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=e−x−cos⁡x.

q-93829.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=-25\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{2x}+Bx{e}^{2x}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=-25\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,y(0)=-3,\,{y}^{′}(0)=5.
$$
q-93829.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ by substituting the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=-3$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & =A{e}^{2(0)}+B(0){e}^{2(0)}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\ -3 & =A-3 \\ A & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $y$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=2A{e}^{2x}+2Bx{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{2x}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=5$ into the derivative gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =2A{e}^{2(0)}+2B(0){e}^{2(0)}+B{e}^{2(0)}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\ 5 & =2A+B+4 \\ 5 & =2(0)+B+4 \\ B & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $A=0$ and $B=1,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
y=x{e}^{2x}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Question 6
?

Given that the differential equation d2ydx2−4dydx+4y=−25cos⁡x

has the general solution y(x)=Ae2x+Bxe2x+4sin⁡x−3cos⁡x,

solve the initial value problem d2ydx2−4dydx+4y=−25cos⁡x,y(0)=−3,y′(0)=5.

a
y=xe2x+4sin⁡x−3cos⁡x
b
y=−xe2x+4sin⁡x−3cos⁡x
c
y=−5xe2x+4sin⁡x−3cos⁡x
d
y=8e2x+4sin⁡x−3cos⁡x
e
y=−2e2x+4sin⁡x−3cos⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We find the constants A and B by substituting the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(0)=−3 into the general solution gives −3=Ae2(0)+B(0)e2(0)+4sin⁡(0)−3cos⁡(0)−3=A−3A=0.

  • Differentiating y gives y′=2Ae2x+2Bxe2x+Be2x+4cos⁡x+3sin⁡x. Substituting y′(0)=5 into the derivative gives 5=2Ae2(0)+2B(0)e2(0)+Be2(0)+4cos⁡(0)+3sin⁡(0)5=2A+B+45=2(0)+B+4B=1.

Finally, since A=0 and B=1, we have the following solution to the initial value problem: y=xe2x+4sin⁡x−3cos⁡x
